description.narrative: Global climate finance remains overwhelmingly centralised, technocratic and inequitable. According to joint analyses by Oxfam and the CARE Climate Justice Centre (2024), nearly 65% of climate funds are provided in the form of loans, exacerbating the debtburden ofdeveloping countries, and less than 10% reaches local actors. In Africa, rural communities – despite being the first victims of climate shocks – receive less than 1.7% of the funding available for adaptation. In Burkina Faso, the deficit is evenmore pronounced: despite ambitious national plans (NDCs,NAPs), municipalities have neither the technical capacity nor the budgetary tools to plan and monitor climate-sensitive spending. Local budgeting remains focused on infrastructure and often ignoresthe dimensions of adaptation,gender and community resilience. An Oxfam study(2023) in the Sahel showed that only 3% of municipal budgets contain a budget line explicitly linked to climate or resilience, even though more than 70% of rural households experience a decline in agricultural productivity due to climate variability. At the same time, gender imbalance in climate governance remains striking. Women and young leaders, although at the heart of local adaptation strategies (agriculture,water management,reforestation), remain under-represented in decision-making and negotiation spaces. In African delegations to UNFCCC conferences, women represent less than30% of negotiators, andyoung women even less than 10%, according to the UN Women report(2023).%,according to the UN Women report (2023). However, initiatives such as the National Academy of Young Climate Negotiators, led by CONAJEC with the support of Oxfam, have demonstrated transformative potential. The 10 young women negotiators trained between 2023 and 2025 actively participated in the COP 28 and COP29 sessionsand the Structured Dialogue on Climate Finance, embodying a new generation of feminist and decolonial diplomats. At the same time, the National Charter of Climate Movements, adopted in 2025bymore than60 civil society organisations, provides a unifying framework for linking citizen mobilisation, political advocacy and climate justice. It is a unique gateway for strengthening civic space, foster local accountability, and promote inclusive and transparent budgets transparent budgets. In this context, the proposed initiative is part of the dynamic of the African Activists for Climate Justice (AACJ) programme and Oxfam's "Climate Finance for the People" initiative. It aims to articulate thedynamics of social movements (National Charter of Climate Movements) and the leadership of young women negotiators to influence:• climate-sensitive local budgets,• national planning and accountability processes,• and regional andinternational political spaces (SB63, COP31, National Green Climate Fund Dialogue).This initiative therefore represents a strategicopportunity to bring together local action,feminist climate diplomacy and inclusive financial governance, in line with the African Union's Vision 2063 andthe priorities of the ministry responsible for climate change, particularly those of Burkina Faso's Directorate-General for the Green Economy and Climate Change (DGEVCC) for the localisation of climate finance

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam Intermón is since 1997 a member of the international Oxfam confederation, sharing values and a strategic plan to achieve greater global impact. Intermón Oxfam fights, with and for disadvantaged populations and as part of a broad global movement, with the aim of eradicating injustice and poverty, and to ensure that all human beings can fully exercise their rights and enjoy a dignified life. Mission, Vision and Values are the components of Oxfam Intermón identity and guide its steps as an organisation and the ideal with which Oxfam Intermón wants to live in order to obtain a fairer world with greater solidarity.
